name: Function notation
definition: Names the output of the function f when the input is x. The parentheses denote evaluation, not multiplication: f(x) is one value determined by x.

examples.explanation: The rule: square the input, then add one.
Evaluating at 3 gives 10.

commonMistakes: Reading f(x) as f times x; the parentheses mean evaluation.

name: Inverse function
definition: Names the function that undoes f: feeding it f(x) returns x. The −1 is notation, not an exponent: f⁻¹(x) is almost never 1/f(x).

examples.explanation: Applying f then its inverse returns the original input.
Inverse sine asks which angle has sine one half.

commonMistakes: Reading f⁻¹ as one over f; only for nonzero numbers does a −1 exponent mean reciprocal.

name: Function composition
definition: Builds a new function by applying g first, then f: (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)). Order matters; f ∘ g usually differs from g ∘ f.
reading: “f composed with g” or “f of g of x”.

examples.explanation: Evaluate g at x, then feed the result into f.

name: Mapping arrow
definition: The plain arrow → states a function's source and target (f: A → B) or a value a limit approaches. The tailed arrow ↦ shows where an individual element goes.

examples.explanation: f takes real inputs to real outputs.
Each x is sent to its square.

contexts.meaning: Domain-to-codomain direction, or element-to-image with the tail.
x → a means x approaches a.

name: Exponential function
definition: The function exp(x) = eˣ with Euler's number as base. It equals its own derivative, which makes it the standard model of proportional growth.
reading: “exp of x” or “e to the x”.

examples.explanation: Any nonzero base to power zero is 1.
The exponential reproduces itself under differentiation.

name: Logarithm
definition: Asks to what power the base b must be raised to get x. Logarithms turn multiplication into addition, which is why they measure orders of magnitude.

examples.explanation: Two cubed is 8.
The product rule for logarithms.

commonMistakes: Writing log(a + b) as log a + log b; the rule applies to products, not sums.

name: Natural logarithm
definition: The logarithm with base e. It is the inverse of the exponential function and the logarithm calculus uses by default.

examples.explanation: e squared needs exponent 2.
The antiderivative of one over x.

name: Sequence term
definition: Names the nth term of a sequence: an ordered list indexed by position. A recurrence relation defines each term from earlier ones.

examples.explanation: The sequence 3, 5, 7, … of odd numbers from 3 up.
Each term is 4 more than the previous one.

name: Summation
definition: Adds many terms compactly. The index below starts the count, the top value ends it, and the expression right of Sigma is the general term.
reading: “the sum from k equals 1 to n of”.

examples.explanation: Add the squares of 1 through 4.

name: Product notation
definition: Multiplies many factors compactly, mirroring summation. The index runs from the lower to the upper value, multiplying each instantiated factor.
reading: “the product from k equals 1 to n of”.

examples.explanation: One times two times three.

name: Binomial coefficient
definition: Counts the ways to choose k objects from n without regard to order: n! / (k!(n−k)!). It also gives the coefficients in the expansion of (a + b)ⁿ.

examples.explanation: Ten pairs can be chosen from five objects.
Binomial coefficients 1, 3, 3, 1 weight the terms.

name: Proportional to
definition: States that one quantity is a constant multiple of another. a ∝ b means a = k·b for some constant k.

examples.explanation: A circle's circumference scales with its radius.

name: Delta (change and discriminant)
definition: Uppercase delta denotes a change in a quantity (Δx), or the discriminant b² − 4ac of a quadratic, whose sign counts real roots.

examples.explanation: The change from x_1 to x_2.
Positive means two real roots, zero one, negative none.

contexts.meaning: Difference between final and initial values.

name: Ellipsis
definition: Three dots marking continuation of a pattern: terms, not written out, follow the established rule. Centered dots suit operations; baseline dots suit lists.

examples.explanation: Add every integer from 1 to 100.

sources.label: OpenStax Precalculus 2e

name: Slope-intercept form
definition: Writes a line with slope m and y-intercept b. Reading m gives steepness; reading b gives where the line crosses the y-axis.

examples.explanation: Slope 2, crossing the y-axis at −1.

sources.label: OpenStax Elementary Algebra 2e

name: Quadratic formula
definition: Solves every quadratic ax² + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0. The ± produces both roots; the expression under the radical is the discriminant.
reading: “x equals negative b plus or minus root b-squared minus 4 a c, over 2 a”.

examples.explanation: For x² + 3x + 2 = 0 this gives x = −1 or x = −2.

sources.label: OpenStax Intermediate Algebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Piecewise definition
definition: Defines a function by different rules on different parts of its domain, grouped by a brace. Each input uses exactly one rule; together the cases must cover every input.

examples.explanation: Nonnegative inputs pass through; negative inputs are negated: the absolute value.

sources.label: OpenStax College Algebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Domain and range
definition: The domain is the set of inputs a function accepts; the range is the set of outputs it produces. Division by zero and even roots of negatives are the usual domain restrictions.

examples.explanation: Square roots of negative numbers are not real, so only nonnegative inputs qualify.

sources.label: OpenStax College Algebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Partial fractions
definition: Splits a rational function into a sum of simpler fractions with linear (or irreducible quadratic) denominators. Each piece integrates or inverts elementarily, which is why the method powers integral calculus and Laplace transforms.

examples.explanation: Check: combining the right side over (x−1)(x+2) gives 1/3·((x+2) − (x−1)) = 1.

sources.label: OpenStax College Algebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Remainder and factor theorems
definition: Dividing a polynomial P by (x − a) leaves remainder P(a). In particular, (x − a) is a factor exactly when P(a) = 0 — evaluation tests divisibility with no division.

examples.explanation: So (x − 2) is a factor; indeed P = (x − 2)(x − 3).
